en: Record of the Method for Contemplating the Mind while Reciting Sutras,
Spoken by the Great Master Tiantai and Recorded by the Venerable Jingxi.
The Great Master, by means of the power of unimpeded eloquence and the power of objectless compassion, benefited sentient beings according to their capacities so that no effort was in vain.

Thus, regarding recitation and study, he established specific skillful means and structural frameworks; while these did not exceed the general principles, the individual items within the detailed system were nonetheless distinct.
Therefore, he further entrusted them with the full range of practices. I, having the honor of inheriting the teachings of this master craftsman, have [studied] them quite extensively...
Synthesizing differences and similarities, one may apply these principles to all matters without exception.

However, because the capacities and conditions of practitioners vary and those who engage in such cultivation are rare, I have briefly indicated the general directions to serve as a guide for practice. Nevertheless, the practical intent of this school necessarily relies upon the ten vehicles.
In this context, although the meaning is sought through the principles until they are sufficient, the specific delineation of the characteristics has not yet been clearly established;

therefore, we shall first indicate the categories of the text regarding the objects of the Truths (*satya*) and establish ten "vehicles" (*yāna*) as a provisional framework. Next, we will extract the essential points from the extensive text.
First, regarding the division of the text, there are three parts within the work itself: the first shows the rules of conduct for body and speech, which constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*).
[This is] the division. The meaning encompasses both self and others. Second, at the bottom of the second [section], it correctly demonstrates contemplation;

this corresponds to one's own practice. Third, at the bottom of the third [section], it concerns circulation; the meaning corresponds to transforming others. Within the correct contemplation, it is divided into two:

first, the method (*dharma*), and second, the meaning (*artha*). "Method" refers to the method of contemplation; "meaning" comprises all practices. The first passage concerns the objective realm (*viṣaya*); the second, starting from "next, must," is...

This is the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Within this, there are also two parts: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion. In the explanation, there are three sections: first, the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*);
second, the contemplation of the lower emptiness; third, although [the self] is non-existent, the middle contemplation. Next, "is able to act" and below is the summary.

Next, "although non-existent" and below clarifies the possession of all practices. Within this, there are again two parts: first, the actual clarification of possessing the dharmas; second, from "from the three... [and so forth].

The world below offers praise and critical appraisal. First, regarding the initial possession of the four dharmas: first, the initial possession of the six perfections; second, the judgment of provisional and ultimate truth in the section beginning with "one's own practice";
third, the possession of the three causes in the section beginning with "if one can"; and fourth, the possession of the three virtues in the section beginning with "if one contemplates.
Within these three virtues, there are both the cultivated and the innate.
Now, those who wish to recite the sutras to extinguish their transgressions must first, above all, wash their hands and rinse their mouths, and maintain a solemn and dignified demeanor.

They should sit cross-legged on a separate seat. Second, they enter into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), visualizing that the seat upon which they sit is high, vast, and magnificent. Next, they visualize that beneath the seat there are devas.
Surrounded by the eight classes of supernatural beings and the fourfold assembly, listen to the Dharma.
Next, you must direct your mind to practice visualization: visualize yourself as a Dharma master who transmits the Buddha’s true teaching and expounds it for the fourfold assembly.
Contemplate the sound that issues forth; it is heard not only by this single assembly, but even throughout the ten directions. This is called "contemplation of the provisional" (jia guan).
Next, contemplate the person who speaks and the sutra they recite: what constitutes the sutra? Is it the physical scroll, or is it the paper?
The ink is the medium; the brush and scroll are the instruments. The sound of recitation issues from the mouth; it arises through the conjunction of the gums and palate.
Is there a self-body? Or is there no self-body? Who is the reciter? Is it the mind that recites, or is it the mouth that recites, or does it arise from their conjunction?
Contemplate these four aggregates: do they truly exist, or do they arise from conceptualization? These four aggregates do not exist; they are without self.
To be able to recite it is called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Although there is no sūtra being recited, there are the sūtra scrolls, paper, ink, and characters; although there is no person who can recite, there is my own body proclaiming it for the fourfold assembly;
although it is neither internal nor external, it is not separate from the internal and external; and although it is not the sūtra itself—
The scroll does not depart from the sutra scroll; although it is neither body nor speech, it does not depart from body and speech. From beginning to end, there is never any discrepancy or error;
this is called the inconceivable. To be able to form this understanding and to be able to form this contemplation is called attaining the three contemplations within a single mind.
They are neither before nor after; the three contemplations are perfectly present.
Although there is no donor, there is the gift of Dharma; although there is no recipient, the fourfold assembly is vividly present;

although there is no Dharma-seat, one ascends the seat to proclaim the teaching. That which is neither one, two, nor three, yet appears as one, two, and three, is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) through the gift of Dharma.
To recite and uphold [the teachings] with single-minded devotion, free from all obstacles, is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To endure evil thoughts and remain undisturbed by fame or material gain is called patience (*kṣānti*). To maintain an uninterrupted focus of mind from beginning to end without any indolence is called diligence (*vīrya*).
This is called diligence (*vīrya*). To single-mindedly contemplate this sutra without attachment to its flavor is called meditation (*dhyāna*).

To discern it without error, thoroughly understanding the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination, with clear and distinct phrasing and wording, is called wisdom (*prajñā*). This is what is meant by the complete fulfillment of the six *pāramitās*.
To practice this sutra oneself is called the Real; to transmit it to others is called the Expedient.
If one can accomplish its merit in a single lifetime, [one will attain liberation].

The mind from beginningless time is called the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); the mind that observes [the truth] is called the cause of realization (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*); and preaching and bestowing [the teaching] upon the fourfold assembly while seated on a high throne is called the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

When the three causes are fully present, if contemplation is not yet clear, it is merely the virtue of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*). By investigating it without ceasing until contemplation and mind are in accord, it is called "entrusting oneself to the holy embryo" (*āryagarbha-pratiṣṭhāna*).
When the karma of the embryo is perfected, it is called the "cultivated virtue" (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). The forty-one intermediate stages are both cultivated and innate.
Upon reaching the ultimate fruit, it is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*). The three dots of the letter *i* are neither vertical nor horizontal; this is called [the *tri-kula*].
The Great Nirvāṇa is called "reaching the other shore" and is called "the emptiness of the ultimate meaning. Equanimous great wisdom is what is meant by reciting the sūtras.
One should correctly contemplate that there are no Buddhas of the three periods of time who do not arise from this. One may give to those who have faith; do not give to those who lack faith.

Third, regarding the dissemination [of the teaching]: if one merely disciplines oneself, it cannot be called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*); if one sees suffering and does not rescue others, it cannot be called "compassion" (*karuṇā*).

Once correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) has been cultivated and manifested before one, one must further adorn the *dharmadhātu*. After finishing the recitation of the sutra and emerging from contemplation, one should employ the merit of this practice with the thought:
"May those who have already attained perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) extensively deliver all sentient beings; may those who have entered the stages..."

All people ascend to the stage of the ground. Those who have not yet entered the stages immediately employ the two dharmas of compassion and loving-kindness, vowing that in future lives they may together achieve perfect enlightenment.

Regarding the subsequent establishment of the ten dharmas: as for the object of contemplation mentioned above, it is the wondrous object. The meaning of cultivating contemplation should be centered in the mind.

Next, one cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); in meaning, this corresponds to *śamatha*. Next, one cultivates the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*); in meaning, this corresponds to "breaking through all" (*póbiàn*). Next, one summarizes and concludes;

in meaning, this corresponds to "penetration and obstruction" (*tōngsè*). Next, one is endowed with the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); in meaning, this corresponds to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). The provisional and the real, as well as the three causes, correspond in meaning to the "primary" and "auxiliary" practices.

Next, one distinguishes between the cultivated nature and the inherent nature; in meaning, this corresponds to the stages and positions (*krama-sthāna*). The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) corresponds in meaning to "patience" (*kṣānti*) and...
By means of non-attachment, one simply relies upon this to practice; it is sufficient for the principle in brief.

However, because the dharmas within the mind have not yet become very clear, the extensive text is further bestowed to assist the practitioner, so that the ten vehicles of contemplation do not go beyond recitation and retention, and the ten objects of contemplation pervade both sound and form. Therefore, it is again elucidated according to the previous precedent.
First, one clearly directs the observation toward the object of contemplation; the nature of the mind and its realm are suchness, embodying the three truths—this is "wondrous.
Second, relying on this wondrous object, one makes vows and recites [the text], seeking the fruit of the three virtues and benefiting sentient beings of the ten realms.

Third, with every phrase and every sentence, one remains mindful without omission; the nature of the mind is luminous, as stillness and illumination operate in tandem. Fourth, through this stillness and illumination...
1. Recite with total integration and universal penetration, encompassing all horizontal and vertical teachings on non-arising. 2. Fifth, when reciting, contemplate the nature of the mind:
although thoughts arise moment by moment, even non-attachment does not exist, so how could attachment possibly exist? 3. Sixth, understand that while reciting, both mind and form are present;

the foundations of mindfulness remain distinct, yet they are tranquil, harmonious, and perfectly balanced in all their aspects. 4. Seventh, during the practice of recitation, if defiled thoughts arise:
Ninth, one should know that although the mind for recitation is complete, once stillness and illumination are spontaneously realized, one has already reached the sixth stage on the path.
Tenth, when circumstances favorable or unfavorable arise during the time of recitation and study, settle them exclusively through stillness and illumination.
Relying on the merit of contemplative recitation, one attains a semblance [of realization]; yet the six sense faculties still crave this semblance-stage, which is called...

Falling from the summit. If one cultivates detachment and enters the Bronze Wheel [Samādhi], yet encounters the King of Karma-Māra, meditative visions, pride, or those who follow the Two Vehicles and are subject to mental agitation, one should immediately shift one’s contemplation and observe them with diligence. As the contemplation of the objects is perfected, one relies on the previous practice of contemplation;
if one does not neglect what has been recited while simultaneously applying this treatment, it is an even more superior technique and the most noble method. Recite!
As it is with the sutras, so it is with the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Nevertheless, they are merely designated as the "Ten Vehicles of Following Practice" (*anugata-daśayāna*);

for full detail, one must ultimately rely upon the great compendiums. Question: What is the difference between the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as prescribed in the great compendiums, and this recitation of the sutras?

Answer: The meaning is the same, but the matter is different. Regarding the difference in matter: because the mere recitation and upholding [of the sutras] is itself virtuous regarding the aggregates. Therefore...
Reciting with body and mouth is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Receiving and apprehending the words and phrases is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Conceptualizing the meaning and flavor is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Performing this recitation and retention is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Discerning them clearly and distinctly is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
These aggregates differ when combined with the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). If one can realize the nature of both matter and mind herein, one shall possess the ten [perfections].

Observing the ten realms without omission, how could this diminish the practice of the Great Vehicle? It differs only in that it integrates ancient and modern perspectives to harmonize the principles of the teachings.
This concludes the *Guanxin songjing fa ji* (Record of the Method for Chanting Sutras through the Contemplation of Mind).
